rows: Construction dust can include silica, wood dust and lower-toxicity dusts.
Employers should assess dust-generating tasks and exposure routes.
Work methods should eliminate or reduce dust generation where practicable.
Water suppression and on-tool extraction can control dust at source.
Extraction equipment should be suitable, maintained and correctly used.
Respiratory protective equipment may be needed for residual exposure.
Workers need training in dust controls and correct RPE use.
Health surveillance may be required where exposure creates an identifiable disease risk.
Visible dust or an issued respirator does not quantify worker exposure.
Conclusions require material, task, duration, controls, extraction performance, RPE fit, housekeeping and exposure evidence.
Cement products can cause skin irritation, dermatitis and serious alkaline burns.
Cement dust can irritate the respiratory system.
Direct skin contact with wet cement should be prevented or minimised.
Work methods and tools should reduce contact and splashing.
Suitable gloves, clothing and eye protection may be required.
Contaminated clothing should be removed and skin washed promptly.
Welfare facilities should support effective washing and skin care.
Workers should receive information about early symptoms and incident response.
Glove use or absence of immediate pain does not prove that cement exposure is controlled.
Conclusions require product, task, contact route, duration, PPE, hygiene, contamination and clinical evidence.
Machinery maintenance should be planned and carried out safely.
Equipment should be shut down and isolated before maintenance where practicable.
Stored energy, gravity, pressure and movement should be released or secured.
Isolation points should be identified and controlled against reconnection.
Access should be prevented to dangerous areas during maintenance.
People carrying out maintenance need suitable competence and instructions.
Guards and protective devices should be restored before return to service.
Testing, restart and handover should follow a controlled process.
A stop button, permit or lock alone does not prove that all energy sources are isolated.
Conclusions require equipment, energy sources, isolation, verification, stored energy, access, competence and restart evidence.
Construction work should be planned to prevent fire and protect people if fire occurs.
Combustible materials and ignition sources should be controlled.
Hot work requires suitable precautions and supervision.
Temporary electrical installations should be safely designed and maintained.
Escape routes and exits should remain available as the site changes.
Fire detection, alarm and firefighting equipment should match the risk.
Workers and visitors should receive site-specific emergency information.
Fire arrangements should be reviewed as structures, occupancy and work phases change.
A fire extinguisher or signed escape route does not prove that construction fire risk is controlled.
Conclusions require materials, ignition, hot work, temporary electrics, alarm, escape, occupancy and emergency-drill evidence.
